outputs.L1:
Wife and servant are the same,  
Distinguished only by the name.  
For once that fatal knot is tied—  
Which nothing, nothing can divide—  
And she has spoken the word “obey,”  
Making man supreme by law that day,  
All kindness then is cast aside,  
And nothing remains but state and pride.  

Fierce as an Eastern prince, he grows  
And all his innate rigor shows.  
A look, a laugh, a word she speaks  
The nuptial contract surely breaks.  
Like mutes, she must communicate through signs,  
And every freedom she resigns;  
Governed always by his nod,  
She must fear her husband as a god.  

Him she must serve, him she must obey,  
And neither act nor ever say  
Anything but what her haughty lord sees fit—  
For he who holds the power claims all the wit.  

Then shun—oh, shun!—that wretched state,  
And all its fawning flatterers hate.  
Value yourselves, and men despise;  
You must be proud if you would be wise.
outputs.L2:
Marriage reduces a woman to servitude, changing only the title by which she is known. Once the supposedly unbreakable bond is formed and she promises obedience, the law places her husband above her. Affection then gives way to arrogance and social rank. He becomes as tyrannical as an Eastern ruler, openly displaying his natural harshness. Even her smallest actions—a glance, a laugh, or a remark—may be treated as violations of their marriage agreement.

She is expected to communicate only through gestures, like someone forbidden to speak, and to surrender every liberty. A mere signal from her husband must direct her conduct, and she must revere and fear him as though he were divine. Her duty is always to attend to him, follow his commands, and neither do nor say anything without her proud master’s approval. Because he possesses authority, he also assumes that he alone possesses judgment.

Therefore, avoid this miserable condition and reject the flattering men who try to lure you into it. Recognize your own worth, scorn men’s pretensions, and preserve your pride—for pride is necessary if you wish to act wisely.
outputs.L3:
The poem portrays marriage as an institution that reduces a wife to the status of a servant, particularly once she vows to obey her husband. Armed with legal authority and personal pride, the husband may become an absolute and harsh ruler within the household. As a result, the wife loses her freedom of expression and action and is expected to submit completely to his wishes.

In response to this unequal relationship, the poem urges women to avoid marriage, distrust the flattering promises of men, and protect their dignity. Rather than presenting pride and independence as faults, it treats them as essential forms of wisdom and self-preservation. By maintaining their autonomy and self-respect, women can resist subordination and retain control over their own lives.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents marriage not as a loving partnership but as an institution that places women in a condition of dependence and servitude. Through satire, the speaker exposes the contradiction between marriage’s idealized image and the harsh reality women may experience within it. A wife is compared to a servant who must obey her husband’s wishes, attend to his needs, and surrender control over her own life. The poem also likens the husband’s authority to that of a tyrant over his subjects, suggesting that the power imbalance within marriage resembles political oppression rather than mutual affection.

These comparisons emphasize how marriage can deprive women of autonomy, equality, and personal dignity. While a servant may at least receive wages or retain some possibility of leaving, a wife is bound by social expectations and legal or moral obligations that make her submission appear natural and permanent. The poem’s satirical tone sharpens this criticism by revealing the absurdity of celebrating an arrangement in which one person gains authority at the expense of another’s freedom.

In its conclusion, the poem directly urges women to recognize their own worth. Rather than accepting male domination or believing that marriage is necessary for happiness and respectability, they should protect their independence and refuse to become subordinate to husbands. Marriage is therefore portrayed as a dangerous loss of freedom rather than a desirable goal. By advising women to avoid the institution altogether, the poem delivers a forceful challenge to patriarchal society and calls on women to preserve their dignity, self-respect, and control over their own lives.

### The Disappointment

One day the amorous Lysander,  
By an impatient passion sway’d,  
Surpris’d fair Cloris, that lov’d maid,  
Who could defend herself no longer.  
All things did with his love conspire;  
The gilded planet of the day,  
In his gay chariot, drawn by fire,  
Was now descending to the sea,  
And left no light to guide the world,  
But what from Cloris’ brighter eyes was hurl’d.

In a lone thicket made for love,  
Silent as yielding maid’s consent,  
She with a charming languishment  
Permits his force, yet gently strove;  
Her hands his bosom softly meet,  
But not to put him back design’d,  
Rather to draw him on inclin’d;  
Whilst he lay trembling at her feet,  
Resistance ’tis in vain to show;  
She wants the power to say—“Ah! What d’ye do?”

Her bright eyes sweet, and yet severe,  
Where love and shame confusedly strive,  
Fresh vigor to Lysander give;  
And whispering softly in his ear,  
She cried—“Cease, cease—your vain desire,  
Or I’ll call out—what would you do?  
My dearer honor, ev’n to you,  
I cannot, must not give—retire,  
Or take that life whose chiefest part  
I gave you with the conquest of my heart.”

But he as much unused to fear,  
As he was capable of love,  
The blessed minutes to improve,  
Kisses her mouth, her neck, her hair;  
Each touch her new desire alarms;  
His burning trembling hand he prest  
Upon her swelling snowy breast,  
While she lay panting in his arms.  
All her unguarded beauties lie  
The spoils and trophies of the enemy.

And now, without respect or fear,  
He seeks the object of his vows,  
(His love no modesty allows)  
And stills her charming murmurs there.  
No sense of shame or sin can move  
Her voice, who breathes her soul in love.  
He saw how at her length she lay,  
He saw her rising bosom bare,  
Her loose thin robes, through which appear  
A shape designed for love and play;  
Abandoned by her pride and shame,  
She does her softest joys dispense,  
Offering her virgin innocence  
A victim to love’s sacred flame;  
While th’ o’er-ravished shepherd lies,  
Unable to perform the sacrifice.

Ready to taste a thousand joys,  
The too transported hapless swain  
Found the vast pleasure turned to pain;  
Pleasure, which too much love destroys!  
The willing garments by he laid,  
And heaven all open to his view;  
Mad to possess, himself he threw  
On the defenceless lovely maid.  
But, oh! what envying god conspires  
To snatch his power, yet leave him the desire?

Nature’s support, without whose aid  
She can no human being give,  
Itself now wants the art to live,  
Faintness its slackened nerves invade:  
In vain th’ enraged youth assayed  
To call his fleeting vigor back,  
No motion ’twill from motion take;  
Excess of love his love betrayed.  
In vain he toils, in vain commands;  
Th’ insensible fell weeping in his hands.

In this so amorous cruel strife,  
Where love and fate were too severe,  
The poor Lysander in despair  
Renounced his reason with his life.  
Now all the brisk and active fire

Served to increase his rage and shame,

Not all her naked charms could move,

### “To the Ladies”  
*Lady Mary Chudleigh (1656–1710)*

Wife and servant are the same,  
But only differ in the name:  
For when that fatal knot is tied,  
Which nothing, nothing can divide:  
When she the word obey has said,  
And man by law supreme has made,  
Then all that’s kind is laid aside,  
And nothing left but state and pride:  
Fierce as an eastern prince he grows,  
And all his innate rigour shows:  
Then but to look, to laugh, or speak,  
Will the nuptial contract break.  
Like mutes she signs alone must make,  
And never any freedom take:  
But still be governed by a nod,  
And fear her husband as her god:  
Him still must serve, him still obey,  
And nothing act, and nothing say,  
But what her haughty lord thinks fit,  
Who, with the power, has all the wit.  
Then shun, oh! shun that wretched state,  
And all the fawning flatterers hate:  
Value yourselves, and men despise:  
You must be proud, if you’ll be wise.

counterfactuals.output:
The lines are from **“The Unequal Fetters”** by **Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea** (1661–1720).

### The Unequal Fetters

Could we stop the time that’s flying,  
Or recall it when ’tis past,  
Put far off the day of dying,  
Or make youth forever last,  
To love would then be worth our cost.

But since we must lose those graces  
Which at first your hearts have won,  
And you seek for in new faces  
When our spring of life is done,  
It would but urge our ruin on.

Free as Nature’s first creation,  
Ere the base laws of servitude  
Brought the world in defamation,  
And subjection multitude,  
We should our hearts more nobly use.

Then shun, oh! shun that wretched state,  
And all the fawning flatterers hate;  
Value yourselves, and men despise:  
You must be proud, if you’ll be wise.
